A Django model manager is the interface through which you query a model’s records. Every model gets a default manager called **objects** that simply returns all rows in the table [2]. The manager’s `get_queryset()` method builds the underlying `QuerySet`; when you call `Model.objects.all()` you are really invoking that manager’s query set.

You write a custom manager when the standard “all objects” query isn’t what you need most of the time. By subclassing `models.Manager` and overriding `get_queryset()` you can return a filtered `QuerySet` that reflects a common business rule. For example, the book defines a `PublishedManager` that limits the query to posts whose `status` is `PUBLISHED` [4]. With this manager you can write `Post.published.all()` to fetch only published posts, keeping the filtering logic in one place.

If you add any custom managers but still want the original “all objects” behavior, you must declare the default manager explicitly (e.g., `objects = models.Manager()`) because the first manager defined becomes the default [1][4]. Thus, you create a custom manager whenever you repeatedly need a specific subset of records or extra query methods that the default manager does not provide.
